CULTURAL HERITAGE
Introduction
11.1.1.1 This section presents the Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment (CHIA) findings of
the Project. The CHIA, which covers Built Heritage Impact Assessment (BHIA) and
Archaeological Impact Assessment (AIA), has been conducted in accordance with
the requirements given in Clause 3.5.11 and Appendix J of the EIA Study Brief (No.
ESB-373/2025).
11.1.1.2 The assessment area for CHIA includes areas within 300m from the Project
Boundary and its associated works. Built heritage and site(s) of archaeological
interest within the 300m assessment area have been identified. The impacts
resulting from the construction and operation of the Project on the identified built
heritage and site(s) of archaeological interest have been assessed. Appropriate
mitigation measures have been proposed to alleviate the impacts as necessary.
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
11.2.1.1 Legislation, standards and guidelines relevant to the CHIA include the following:
• Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499);
• Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-
TM) Annexes 10 and 19; and
• Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (A&MO) (Cap. 53).
Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499) and EIAO-TM
Annexes 10 and 19
11.2.1.2 According to Schedule 1 of the EIAO, Site of Cultural Heritage refers to “an
antiquity or monument, whether being a place, building, site or structure or a relic,
as defined in the Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (Cap. 53) and any place,
building, site, or structure or a relic identified by the Antiquities and Monuments
Office to be of archaeological, historical or palaeontological significance.”1
11.2.1.3 Annexes 10 and 19 of EIAO-TM provide the criteria and guidelines for evaluating
the impacts to Sites of Cultural Heritage. It is stated in Annex 10 that adverse
impacts to Sites of Cultural Heritage shall be kept to an absolute minimum and that
the general presumption of impact assessment shall be in favour of the protection
and conservation of all Sites of Cultural Heritage. Annex 19 provides the commonly
adopted approaches and methodologies for assessment of impact on Sites of
Cultural Heritage.
Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (A&MO) (Cap. 53)

historical, archaeological and paleontological interest and for matters ancillary
thereto or connected therewith. The Ordinance contains the statutory procedures

11.3.1.6 Based on the results of the baseline study and archaeological survey, an

Project Background
11.4.1.1 The Northern Metropolis Highway - San Tin Section is situated in the northeast of
Yuen Long District. It is an approximately 9-kilometre-long carriageway stretching
from Au Tau (凹頭) to Pak Shek Au (白石凹), connecting the Tin Shui Wai Section
and Kwu Tung Section of NMH. The Project passes through areas near Ngau Tam
Mei (牛潭尾) and San Tin (新田). It also leads to Kam Tin (錦田) by connecting with
Tsing Long Highway (青朗公路). Figure 11.1 presents the Project area and the
300m assessment area for CHIA.
11.4.1.2 This section presents the geographical, historical and archaeological information of
the Project area and its 300m assessment area. For ease of discussion, the
following sections are discussed according to the areas along the Project alignment
from south to north, namely Au Tau, Ngau Tam Mei and San Tin.
Geographical and Geological Background
Physical Geography
11.4.1.3 The alignment begins at the interchange of Yuen Long Highway / Tsing Long
Highway. It traverses low-lying areas near Au Tau and runs along the western
foothill of Kai Kung Leng (雞公嶺) which separates the Kam Tin plain and Ngau Tam
Mei river valley. The alignment continues to the north and passes through Ngau
Tam Shan (牛潭山) and Ki Lun Shan (麒麟山). Eventually, it reaches Pak Shek Au
in the North District.
• Au Tau
11.4.1.4 The alignment connects with the Tin Shui Wai Section at the mouth of the Kam Tin
(錦田) plain where the Kam Tin River discharges into Deep Bay. The area is
surrounded by a large area of fishponds in Nam Sang Wai and Au Tau to the west,
the lower foothills of Kai Kung Leng to the east, and Kam Tin River and Ho Hok
Shan (蠔殼山) to the south. The landscape along the alignment transitions from
low-lying wetlands and river plains near Kam Tin River in the south to the hill slopes
of Kai Kung Leng in the north.

11.4.1.5 The terrain in this section is predominantly flat lowland, particularly in the vicinity of
Tung Shing Lei (東成里), Sha Po Tsuen (沙埔村) and Mo Fan Heung (模範鄉).
These low-lying areas generally have terrestrial elevations ranging from
approximately +2mPD to +27mPD, with gradients of <1° to about 15°
. Towards the
foothills of Kai Kung Leng and Ho Hok Shan, the terrain becomes uneven with
elevations rising to over +160mPD and +80mPD respectively, and gradients
exceeding 35° and 27° respectively.
• Ngau Tam Mei
11.4.1.6 The alignment proceeds along the northern hillslopes of Kai Kung Leng on the
southern edge of the Ngau Tam Mei river valley. It passes through the low-lying
areas near Ngau Tam Mei Water Treatment Works, then heads east into the hill
ranges of Ngau Tam Shan.
11.4.1.7 The terrain in this section is primarily rugged and uneven with steeper slopes and
higher elevations as the alignment moves into the hill ranges of Kai Kung Leng and
Ngau Tam Shan. These hill ranges near the alignment raise to elevations between
approximately +20mPD and +337mPD, with gradients ranging from about 10° to
38°. Nevertheless, low-lying fishponds and agricultural fields with gently sloping
terrain can still be found in the Ngau Tam Mei river valley. These low-lying areas
near the alignment are elevated between approximately +7mPD and +30mPD with
gradient of <1° to about 10°
.
• San Tin
11.4.1.8 The alignment continues northwards along the hill ranges of Ki Lun Shan before
crossing Fanling Highway and finishing at Pak Shek Au. An interchange connecting
to the San Tin river valley is proposed at Saddle Pass (麒麟山坳), which also slightly
encroaches into Ki Lun Tsuen (麒麟村) to the east of the Saddle Pass.
11.4.1.9 The terrain in this section is hilly as the alignment traverses along the hill ridges of
Ki Kun Shan, with the San Tin river valley to the west and Sheung Rue River valley
to the east. The terrestrial elevation around Ki Lun Shan ranges between
approximately +30mPD and +210mPD, while it drops to about +40mPD at Saddle
Pass. The low-lying plains of the San Tin river valley around the vicinity of the
alignment is elevated between approximately +12mPD and +35mPD, while those
of Ki Lun Tsuen range between approximately +12mPD and +36mPD. Gradients
of the low-lying plains are generally between <1° and 10°, whereas those of Ki Lun
Shan vary between 10° and 38°.
11.4.1.10 The alignment ends at Pak Shek Au, which is a gap between Ki Lun Shan in the
south and Mount Kirkpatrick and Tit Hang Shan (鐵坑山) in the north where the
Fanling Highway is located. The elevation rises again to the north as the alignment
approaches Mount Kirkpatrick and Tit Hang Shan. Elevations in areas north of
Fanling Highway range roughly from +6mPD to +127mPD. Gradient of this section
is roughly between <1° and 23° while slopes on Mount Kirkpatrick and Tit Hang
Shan rises to over 30°.

11.4.1.11 Past landscape before modern development can be revealed from geology 2
.
Referring to Figure 11.2, the landscape of the Project is comprised of hill ranges,
river valleys and coastal environment.
• Au Tau
11.4.1.12 The alignment begins at the mouth of Kam Tin river valley. The surrounding
watershed, including Ho Hok Shan and Kai Kung Leng, are primarily composed of
volcanic rocks (JTM) formed during the Upper Jurassic period. These bedrocks are
covered by debris flow deposits (Qpd) formed during the Pleistocene along the hill
slopes.
11.4.1.13 River running in the Kam Tin valleys during the Pleistocene formed the second river
terrace, as characterised by terraced alluvium deposits (Qpa). The first river terrace
was formed later during the Holocene due to a drop in sea level at around 6,000BP3
,
as represented by the alluvium deposits (Qa). The edge between the offshore
seabed of the Deep Bay and the first river terrace delineates the past coastline
before modern urban development, evidenced by the presence of marine mud
(QHH) and alluvium deposits (Qa) within the assessment area.
11.4.1.14 The geology of the alignment near Au Tau is largely composed of marine mud
(QHH), reflecting a coastal environment. The geology is then transitioned to
volcanic rocks (JTM), debris flow deposits (Qpd) and terraced alluvium deposits
(Qpa) as the alignment approaches the foothills of Kai Kung Leng into a more
terrestrial landscape.
• Ngau Tam Mei
11.4.1.15 The alignment near Ngau Tam Mei primarily traverses hilly terrain, passing through
the slopes of Kai Kung Leng and Ngau Tam Shan. Same as Kai Kung Leng, Ngau
Tam Shan is composed of volcanic rocks (JTM) formed during the Upper Jurassic
period, while its hillslopes are formed by debris flow deposits (Qpd) formed during
the Pleistocene.
11.4.1.16 The ridgelines of Kai Kung Leng and Ngau Tam Shan define the west-facing Ngau
Tam Mei river valley. Evidence of river activity during the Pleistocene is seen in the
terraced alluvium deposits (Qpa), which mark the second river terrace. The first
river terrace formed during the Holocene when the sea level dropped at around
6,000BP, as indicated by the alluvium deposits (Qa).
11.4.1.17 As the alignment crosses the Ngau Tam Mei river valley near the hillslopes, the
geology of the alignment here is dominated by volcanic rocks (JTM) and debris flow
deposits (Qpd).
• San Tin
11.4.1.18 The alignment continues northward from Ngau Tam Shan to the hill ranges of Ki
Lun Shan. Ki Lun Shan shares the same geological composition as Ngau Tam
Shan and Kai Kung Leng. It was formed during Upper Jurassic period (JTM) as
part of the Tai Mo Shan Formation with debris flow deposits (Qpd) as slopes.

Human Geography – Village Settlement
• Au Tau
11.4.1.20 Areas near at the mouth of Kam Tin river valley and Fung Kat Heung (逢吉鄉) had
traditionally been used as cultivation fields in the early 20th century4
. Village
settlements in this area are established relatively recent. Backed by the northern
foothills of Ho Hok Shan, a neighbourhood named Tung Shing Lei was established
between 1919 and 19355
. Other village settlements, including Fung Kat Heung, Mo
Fan Heung and Wah Shing Village (華盛村), are located at the bottom of the
southwest hillslopes of Kai Kung Leng.
• Ngau Tam Mei
11.4.1.21 Traditional and well-established villages, such as Pok Wai (壆圍), are located at the
former coastline before modern development. The plains with the valley in Ngau
Tam Mei used to be cultivated by the Punti (本地) people from San Tin 6
.
11.4.1.22 In the early 20th century, Hakka people from Boluo (博羅), Huizhou (惠州) and
Dongguan (東莞) in the Guangdong Province moved in and rented the lands from
the Punti to establish settlements and agriculture activities 7. More villages were
established in the Ngau Tam Mei river valley between the late 19th century and mid-
20th century, including Yau Tam Mei Tsuen (攸潭美村), San Wai Tsuen (新圍村)
and Long Ha (朗廈). They generally occupied areas in the mouth of the Ngau Tam
Mei river valley close to the coast8. In the 1960s, these settlements had expanded
further to the east of the valley 9 10
.
11.4.1.23 Towards the 21st century, some of the village area along San Tin Highway have
been redeveloped into modern low-density private housings.

Historical Background
Qin to Yuan Dynasties (221BC to AD1368)
11.4.1.31 Clues of human occupation within the south China can be found in historic textual
records such as Shiji (史記) and Hanshu (漢書), written in the first century BC and
first century AD respectively. These records describe that Yue ethnic groups (also
known as Hundreds of Yue (百越)) were scattered in southern China. The Yue
ethnic groups were comprised of different tribes bearing various surnames and can
be differentiated from the Han ethnic group who lived in central China in terms of
physical characteristics, language, and folklore.
11.4.1.32 The Yue people were gradually assimilated into the Han culture when southern
China became an administration territory of the central government since Qin
dynasty (221BC to 206BC). During the Qin period, the Guangdong region was
subordinated to Panyu (番禺) County. In 208BC, Southern Yue State (南越國) was
established around the Guangdong region by military officials, who were sent from
the Qin Court to conquer the Yue in the south. Following the collapse of Qin’s
political power in the north, Han dynasty (206BC to AD220)31 began. Southern Yue
State was soon becoming a vassal state of Han before integrated into the Han
Empire.
11.4.1.33 Between Han and Eastern Jin dynasties (AD317 to AD420), Hong Kong was
subordinated to Boluo (博羅) County32. From AD331 to AD756, Hong Kong was
subordinated to Bao’an (寶安) County. After AD757, Hong Kong was subordinated
to Dongguan (東莞) County and followed by Song dynasty (AD960 to AD1279) and
Yuan dynasty (AD1271 to AD1368)33
.

Summary and Interpretation of Archaeological Field Survey Results
Test Pit Excavation
11.6.1.5 Two (2) test pits and two (2) auger holes, along with field scanning were conducted
at Ngau Tam Mei SAI. The test pit excavations aimed to establish the horizontal
spread of cultural layers and the depth of cultural layers (if any), as well as to
discover the presence of any buried archaeological remains. The test pits were
excavated with dimensions of 2.0m by 1.0m with vertical test pit walls and
rectangular shape in plan. The locations of the two test pits, namely NTM-TP1 and
NTM-TP2 (where NTM and TP stand for “Ngau Tam Mei SAI” and “Test Pit”,
respectively), are shown in Figure 11.7.
11.6.1.6 Both test pits were placed to ensure the archaeological significance could be
discerned from the proposed location. Test pits were placed in a North-South
orientation to facilitate field recording. Excavation of NTM-TP1 was carried out
using hand-held tools and extended down to the sterile layer. Hand-held auger hole
drilling was performed on NTM-TP1 upon reaching the bottom of the test pit and in
proximity to verify that the excavation reached the sterile layer. Attempts were made
to excavate NTM-TP2, but since there was a concrete surface exposed after
removing the top soil, in-depth excavation and augering were interrupted.
11.6.1.7 No artefact was identified in both NTM-TP1 and NTM-TP2. Stratigraphy and record
for the concerned test pits and auger holes are presented in Appendix 11.2 Test
Pit and Auger Hole Records. The findings of the two test pits are discussed below.
Findings from NTM-TP1 and NTM-TP2
11.6.1.8 NTM-TP1 was located on the gentle slope in front of Sun Hing Farm (新興農場),
while NTM-TP2 was located in adjacent to the concrete road connecting to the farm.
11.6.1.9 NTM-TP1 consisted of two (2) major strata in five (5) contexts, reflecting the natural
and human events that took place in this area. NTM-AH1 (AH stands for “Auger
Hole”) was drilled in proximity to a depth of 1.2 m that showed an identical context.
An auger hole was also drilled at the base of NTM-TP1 further down 0.43 m at a
depth of 1.63 m when it encountered rocks.
• Context NTM-TP1-C1 to NTM-TP1-C4: Modern deposit
o No artefacts were identified in this stratum;
o NTM-TP1-C1 was modern fill soil that contained frequent refuse and humus;
o NTM-TP1-C2 was modern agricultural soil containing frequent roots;
o NTM-TP1-C3 was modern agricultural soil that contained occasional
weathered rocks.; and
o NTM-TP1-C4 is a cut likely showing a dug pit of Context NTM-TP1-C3 could
be observed at the south profile in this context.
• Context NTM-TP1-C5: Sterile. The test pit ended at 1.2 m depth, and auger
hole drilling revealed the same deposit as Context NTM-AH1-C4.
o No artefacts were identified in this stratum; and
o NTM-TP1-C5 was a firm dark brown silty clay that contained occasional
weathered rocks. It represented the slope deposit of colluvial soil commonly
seen in this region. This context was also the limit of excavation.

depth of approximately 0.8m (i.e. Context NTM-TP1-C1 to NTM-TP1-C3), as told

had taken place, with occasional roots observed since Context NTM-TP1-C3. A
dug pit (i.e. Context NTM-TP1-C4 (Cut)) appeared as U-shape in the south profile

location. The soil profile of Context NTM-TP1-C3 likely indicated that the
agricultural fields were extracted and transferred from slope deposit of colluvial soil
in other locations and disposed, placing on top of the sterile layer. Such agricultural
activities were evident in aerial photos from the 1960s 60. After the abandonment

to fruit trees planting, forming Context NTM-TP1-C2 that contained frequent roots.

finalisation of the Project design and land resumption arrangements.

Conclusion
11.7.1.1 The baseline study, comprising desktop research and field evaluation, has identified
thirteen (13) graded historic buildings within the assessment area of the Project but
outside the Project Boundary. The five (5) Grade 2 historic buildings and eight (8)
Grade 3 historic buildings are situated at a considerable distance from the Project
Boundary. Therefore, no impact to them during the construction and operation
phases. No declared monument, proposed monument, new item for grading
assessment and Government historic site is located within the assessment area.
Therefore, no impact is anticipated to the built heritage during the construction and
operation phases. As no impact on built heritage is anticipated during the
construction and operation phases, no mitigation measure is required.
11.7.1.2 For archaeology, Ngau Tam Mei SAI is partially located within the Project Boundary.
The archaeological survey conducted at this stage indicates that the area in the
vicinity of NTM-TP1 has experienced modern disturbance, with a lack of
archaeological findings that suggests low archaeological significance. On the other
hand, the existing concrete surface encountered at NTM-TP2 has hindered the
identification of archaeological significance underlying the concrete surface of this
area at the current stage.
11.7.1.3 Ngau Tam Mei SAI lies partially within the Project Boundary. The proposed works
carried out within the SAI would only be temporary works that will not cause soil
disturbance and therefore no impact is anticipated. Contractors will be required to
submit method statements for approval by AMO and maintain photographic records
of ground conditions, before, during and after works. With the control measures in
place, the Project is expected to proceed with no impact to the Ngau Tam Mei SAI
during the construction phase. Moreover, impact to archaeology during operation
phase is not anticipated.

of works, so that appropriate mitigation measures, if needed, can be formulated in
a timely manner and implemented in agreement with and to the satisfaction of AMO.
